intro: A story from 1843 opens with a man insisting he is not mad, and every sentence he adds to prove it makes you surer that he is. That gap, between what a text says and what it means, is where literature does its most interesting work. This unit begins with the tools writers use to open that gap and the tools readers use to cross it: structure, unreliable narration, irony, ambiguity, satire, motif, symbol, archetype, allusion, and the stream of a mind on the page. You will also learn what to do when two careful readers see different things in the same lines, and how to write an interpretation that argues instead of reporting.

The second half of the unit turns those tools on three centuries of American writing, from a Puritan woman's love poem in 1650 to a Black poet's mask in 1895. Bradstreet, Edwards, Paine, Emerson, Thoreau, Hawthorne, Poe, Melville, Whitman, Dickinson, Douglass, Jacobs, Twain, Crane, Chopin, London, Wharton and Dunbar did not write in isolation. They read one another and argued back. The preacher who threatened hell is answered by the boy who chooses it for a friend. The essayist who said trust yourself is answered by a sea that does not care what you trust.

By the end you will be able to name a device and, more importantly, say what it does; to weigh two readings of a text and defend the stronger; and to hear American literature as a long conversation about what this country is and who it includes. Every writer here is public domain, which means every text is free to you, and the argument they started is one you are allowed to join.
bigQuestion: How do writers make texts mean more than they say, and how have American writers used that power to argue about what America is?

timeline.t: Anne Bradstreet's The Tenth Muse is printed in London, the first published book of poems by a colonial American
Jonathan Edwards preaches Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God at Enfield, Connecticut
Thomas Paine publishes Common Sense in January and the first American Crisis in December
Edgar Allan Poe publishes The Tell-Tale Heart, told by a narrator who insists he is not mad
Frederick Douglass publishes his Narrative, written by himself
Thoreau's Civil Disobedience is printed, three years after his night in the Concord jail
Herman Melville's Moby-Dick opens with the words Call me Ishmael
Walt Whitman prints the first Leaves of Grass without his name on the cover
Harriet Jacobs publishes Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl as Linda Brent
Adventures of Huckleberry Finn is published in the United States
Paul Laurence Dunbar publishes We Wear the Mask; Stephen Crane publishes The Red Badge of Courage

words.d: a storyteller whose account the reader has reason to doubt, by the author's design
a gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows
deliberate openness to two or more meanings, each supported by the text
writing that attacks a folly, vice or institution by making it look ridiculous
an object, image, phrase or sound that repeats through a text and gathers meaning
a brief reference to a person, event or text outside the work that carries its meaning into the work
narration that reproduces the flow of a character's thoughts, with jumps and missing connectors
clear, direct writing that avoids ornament in order to serve truth
Emerson, Thoreau and their circle, who held that truth comes through the individual's intuition and conscience
a first-person account of life in slavery and escape from it, published to argue against slavery
a movement after the Civil War aiming to show ordinary life and speech truthfully
a movement showing people shaped by forces beyond their control: nature, society, heredity and chance

test.q: A narrator describes his careful planning of a murder as proof of his sanity. What should a reader do with that account?
choices: Accept it, since the narrator was there
Read against it, using his own details as evidence of the opposite
Skip it and read the ending
Assume the author made a mistake
test.why: An unreliable narrator's slips are evidence the author planted for the reader.

test.q: A story begins with a wedding and then goes back twenty years to show how the couple met. The opening is an example of
test.why: Starting in the middle of the action and then going back is in medias res.

test.q: A man sells his watch to buy combs for his wife, who has sold her hair to buy him a watch chain. This is
test.why: The gap is between what was expected and what happened, not in anyone's words.

test.q: Which is the best test for whether a passage is ambiguous rather than vague?
choices: Each of its possible meanings is supported by specific lines
The author refused to explain it
test.why: Ambiguity means supported multiple meanings; vagueness means no clear meaning.

test.q: The real target of Swift's A Modest Proposal is
choices: landlords and policies that were devouring the Irish poor
test.why: The cannibal proposal is the tool; the treatment of the poor is the target.

test.q: A red scarf appears in six scenes of a novel and is finally burned. The scarf is best described as
choices: a motif that becomes a symbol
test.why: It repeats (motif) and comes to stand for something (symbol).

test.q: 'Call me Ishmael' tells a reader who knows the Bible that the narrator is
test.why: The biblical Ishmael was cast out and lived; the allusion brings that meaning to the narrator.

test.q: When two readings of a text conflict, the stronger one
choices: explains more of the text with less strain and survives its best objection
is the one with more literary terms
is the one the teacher prefers
test.why: Coverage, evidence and survival under objection are the tests.

choices: a real person keeping both her faith and her own voice inside a rigid system
test.why: Her plain, personal poems hold faith and worldly love in tension.

test.q: Which pair matches a writer to the earlier writer he most directly answers, according to the unit?
choices: Thoreau answers Edwards on the authority of conscience
Crane answers Bradstreet on free verse
test.why: Edwards would terrify the conscience into submission; Thoreau makes it the highest authority.

test.q: Whitman's free verse and Dickinson's compressed lines both
choices: were widely published in their lifetimes
answer Emerson's call to trust the self and invent a form for it
test.why: Opposite in size and reach, both poets built new forms around the self.

test.q: Douglass's Narrative makes the story of learning to read central because
choices: it shows that slavery depended on keeping minds in the dark
the book was written for children
test.why: The master's fear of a literate slave told Douglass what freedom required.

test.q: Harriet Jacobs hid for nearly seven years in a garret in order to
choices: escape her owner and stay near her children
wait for the Civil War to end
test.why: The hiding place kept her near her children and out of her owner's reach.

test.q: Huck Finn's 'All right, then, I'll go to hell' is dramatic irony because
choices: the reader knows Huck is choosing good while Huck believes he is choosing sin
Twain says so in a footnote
test.why: The gap between Huck's knowledge and the reader's accuses the society that taught him.

test.q: Which writer is described as the hinge between Douglass's generation and the Harlem Renaissance?
test.why: Dunbar met Douglass in Chicago in 1893 and his mask poem was carried forward by Hughes's generation.

write.prompt: Choose two writers from this unit who disagree about the self, the individual conscience or what America is (for example Emerson and Crane, Edwards and Twain, or Douglass and Jacobs). Make a claim about what the later writer is answering in the earlier one, support it with specific evidence from both, and explain what the disagreement reveals.
tips: Your claim must be about the relationship: not 'both write about the self' but 'X answers Y by showing that...'
Quote or describe at least one specific passage from each writer; keep quotations short and public domain.
After each piece of evidence, write two or three sentences of reasoning that connect it to your claim.
State the strongest objection to your reading fairly, then show what it cannot explain.
Keep both writers in play in every paragraph; a comparison that drops one writer becomes a report.
